title: Count Symmetric Integers
description:
# Count Symmetric Integers

An integer is called symmetric if both conditions hold:

* it has an even number of decimal digits; and
* the sum of the digits in the first half equals the sum of the digits in the second half.

Given two integers `low` and `high`, return the number of symmetric integers in the inclusive range `[low, high]`.

Numbers with an odd number of digits are never symmetric.

## Example 1

**Input**
low = 1, high = 100

**Output**
9

**Explanation**
The symmetric integers in the range are `11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88, 99`.

## Example 2

**Input**
low = 1200, high = 1230

**Output**
4

**Explanation**
The symmetric integers are `1203, 1212, 1221, 1230`.

## Constraints

* `1 <= low <= high <= 100000`

tests.description: sample four-digit range with matching half sums
all two-digit repeated numbers are symmetric
four-digit boundary with equal half sums
largest four-digit repeated number is symmetric
five-digit numbers are odd length and 100000 is not symmetric
range crossing from two to three digits should count only 99
several four-digit values can match the same left-half sum

solutions.name: String Enumeration
solutions.description:
## Approach
Enumerate every value in `[low, high]`, convert it to a decimal string, and skip odd lengths. For even lengths, sum digits in the first half and second half and compare the two sums.

## Key Insight
The definition is written in terms of decimal digits, so the string form gives the clearest baseline. The midpoint of an even-length string is the exact boundary between the two halves.

## Complexity Analysis
Each number contributes up to `d` digit operations, where `d` is the number of decimal digits, so the time complexity is O((high - low + 1) * d). The string representation stores O(d) characters, so the space complexity is O(d).

solutions.name: Numeric Digit Split
solutions.description:
## Approach
Check each number arithmetically. First count its digits. If the count is even, peel off the right half with `% 10` and `/ 10`, then sum the remaining left half and compare.

## Key Insight
This is the same half-sum test without building a string. Removing the right half first leaves the left half in the remaining integer, so the two sums can be computed with constant extra memory.

## Complexity Analysis
Each number is divided by 10 a constant number of times per digit, so the time complexity is O((high - low + 1) * d). Only counters are used, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Digit Length Casework
solutions.description:
## Approach
Use the input bound to handle only possible even digit lengths. Two-digit numbers are symmetric when their tens and ones digits match; four-digit numbers compare the sum of the first two digits with the sum of the last two.

## Key Insight
Within `1..100000`, the only useful even digit lengths are 2 and 4. One-, three-, and five-digit numbers are odd length, and `100000` has unequal half sums.

## Complexity Analysis
Every value in the range is checked with constant-time arithmetic, so the time complexity is O(high - low + 1). The algorithm stores only counters and digit sums, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: Prefix Count Table
solutions.description:
## Approach
Precompute `prefix[value]`, the number of symmetric integers from `1` through `value`. After the table is built, answer the interval with `prefix[high] - prefix[low - 1]`.

## Key Insight
Many range-counting problems can be turned into prefix counts. Even though there is only one query here, this route teaches the reusable pattern and separates the symmetric-number predicate from the interval subtraction.

## Complexity Analysis
The table checks every value up to `high`, and each check scans its digits, so the time complexity is O(high * d). The prefix table stores `high + 1` integers, so the space complexity is O(high).
